findings.title: removeStoredCredentialById does not work for federated recovery codes credential
findings.body: After switching from `getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream` (local-only) to `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` (federated-first, then local), the authenticator still calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`. `removeStoredCredentialById` only removes from local Keycloak storage, so when the recovery codes credential lives in user/federated storage and all codes are used, the credential is never removed from the user storage. Result: spent codes remain valid in the user storage backend (any code still in the list can still be presented and matched by `isValid`); only the required-action fallback masks the problem. This is a regression introduced by the diff at line 80 vs. the original.

findings.title: NPE in getCredentials when user is unknown to storage
findings.body: The new `getCredentials` override stores the lookup in `var myUser = getMyUser(user);` and then dereferences `myUser.recoveryCodes` (and `myUser.otp`) without a null check. `getMyUser` returns `null` whenever the user is not in the in-memory map, so any call for a non-existent user (e.g., lookup paths that probe storage) throws NullPointerException. The earlier code path went through `AbstractUserAdapterFederatedStorage`'s default `getCredentials`, which tolerated missing users. Either guard with `if (myUser != null)` or match the previous null-tolerant behavior.

findings.title: disableCredentialType silently ignores recovery-codes and leaks stale codes
findings.body: `disableCredentialType` was extended to support OTP but not `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE`. Calling `user.disableCredentialType([RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE])` (e.g., from admin REST or `UserResource.disableCredentialType`) returns without doing anything for this storage, but the admin endpoint reports success. The recovery codes remain usable in the user storage. The parallel `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` (line 254) was also not updated to advertise recovery-codes as a disableable type, so the admin console still lists it. Both pieces must be updated together so disabling the credential actually removes/clears it and so admins can see it as disableable.

findings.title: NoSuchElementException when user has no recovery codes
findings.body: The constructor calls `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user).get()` directly. If the user has no recovery codes credential (in either federated or local storage), `Optional.get()` throws `NoSuchElementException` and the login form rendering for the recovery code page fails. The bean should check `isPresent()` and render gracefully (e.g., the page should not be shown at all, or the bean should provide a default) instead of throwing. This was previously masked by `getStoredCredentialsByTypeStream(...).findFirst().get()` with the same risk; the refactor was a chance to fix it.

findings.title: Typo in authenticator config alias
findings.body: In `configureBrowserFlowWithRecoveryAuthnCodes`, the alias is set to `"delayed-suthenticator-config"` (sic). The authenticator provider id just above is `"delayed-authenticator"`, so the alias should be `"delayed-authenticator-config"`. The typo makes the test config alias inconsistent with the provider it configures and is misleading when debugging the flow.

findings.title: Unnecessary credential provider lookup when user storage handles recovery codes
findings.body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` always calls `session.getProvider(CredentialProvider.class, "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes")` at line 116, but the provider is only needed in the `else` branch when `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` returns false. When the user storage does accept the credential, this provider lookup is wasted. Move the provider lookup into the `else` branch to avoid the unnecessary work; this also matches the cleaner conditional pattern.

findings.title: Raw recovery codes passed to user storage instead of hashed values
findings.body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` serializes the raw, unhashed `generatedCodes` to JSON and hands them to `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` via the third constructor argument of `UserCredentialModel`. The user storage is then expected to persist them; nothing in this helper forces or even encourages the user storage to hash them. Meanwhile, the local-storage path passes the `credentialModel` (which `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`/the recovery-codes provider hashes internally). The new test `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage` follows this contract literally and stores raw codes as plaintext (`setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())`), so any user storage that follows the same pattern will end up with raw recovery codes in their backend. Consider passing already-hashed values (the same set the local provider would persist) to the user storage so both paths store hashed values, and/or document the requirement that user storage providers must hash before persisting.

findings.title: NPE risk when generated-codes hidden field is missing
findings.body: `processAction` does `generatedCodesString.equals(...)`, `generatedAtTimeString.equals(...)`, and `generatedCodesString.split(",")` without null-checking `generatedCodesString` or `generatedAtTimeString`. If the form is submitted without those hidden inputs (or with empty values), `NullPointerException` is thrown and the user is bounced back via the default error path instead of the deliberate "authn codes have been tampered" branch. Guard against null/empty before calling `.equals(...)`/`.split(...)`.
